title: PrinterThreeDClear
question: How does a 3D printer work?
hook: A 3D printer cannot draw a shape. It can only draw one thin slice, then another on top. Slice a model, watch plastic melt through a 0.4 mm nozzle, steer a printer three ways, and break a print on purpose.

explainer.title: A stack of slices
explainer.text: A printer cannot print a shape. A program called a slicer cuts the model into flat layers, typically 0.1 to 0.3 mm thick for plastic, and plans the path the nozzle follows in each one. Every layer gets perimeters for the walls, solid skin on the top and bottom, and sparse infill inside. Where a layer would hang in the air, the slicer adds supports to snap away later.

explainer.title: Filament in, plastic out
explainer.text: Most desktop printers melt a plastic string 1.75 mm thick. A stepper-driven gear pushes the filament into a heater block, about 190 to 230 °C for PLA and 230 to 250 °C for PETG. The solid filament is the piston: it pushes the melt through a nozzle with a hole usually 0.4 mm wide. Feed too fast or run too cold and the heater cannot melt plastic quickly enough, so the gear skips.

explainer.title: A robot that counts steps
explainer.text: Stepper motors turn in small exact steps, so the printer can count steps to know where each part is. Belts slide the head and the bed, and lead screws lift the gantry one layer at a time. The bed is heated, around 55 to 60 °C for PLA and 70 to 90 °C for PETG, to keep the first layer stuck and the part from curling.

explainer.title: Three ways to move
explainer.text: A Cartesian printer has one motor per axis. A CoreXY printer keeps the bed still, and two fixed motors drive belts that combine: together they move the head sideways, in opposition forwards. A delta printer hangs the nozzle from three arms on three towers, and the controller solves the geometry for each point.

explainer.title: Why prints fail
explainer.text: Plastic shrinks as it cools, so cold beds let corners curl up. Runny plastic oozes during travel moves and leaves strings, which retraction and a cooler nozzle reduce. An overhang droops when each layer is laid mostly over air: the overlap with the layer below is 1 minus layer height times the tangent of the angle, divided by the bead width. A fan lets steeper angles print.

explainer.title: Light, powder and metal
explainer.text: Resin printers harden liquid photopolymer with light from a laser or a projector, and the part hangs upside down from a plate that lifts a layer at a time. Powder printers fuse a thin layer of nylon with a laser, drop the bed and spread more. The loose powder supports the part. Metal printers melt metal powder under argon and weld the part to a plate with supports.

The thickness of one layer. Thinner layers hide the steps but need many more of them.
A loop of plastic following the outline of a layer. Several together make the wall.
A sparse pattern inside the walls that holds them apart for much less plastic.
Throw-away material printed under an overhang so the layer above has something to sit on.
The plastic string, usually 1.75 mm thick, that a filament printer melts and lays down.
